interactions: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole + metformin: trimethoprim inhibits the renal tubular secretion of metformin, raising its levels; with reduced renal function this adds to the risk of lactic acidosis; withhold metformin while creatinine is raised.

warnings: Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubular sodium channel: it can cause hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, and raises serum creatinine by inhibiting its tubular secretion without a true fall in GFR.

output.query: Treatment of hyponatremia presenting with seizures; limits of sodium correction

results.finding: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia, including seizures, is treated with 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice while checking sodium, aiming for a rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour.
The rise in sodium should not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further 24 hours.
In patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination (sodium 105 mmol/L or below, hypokalemia, alcohol misuse, malnutrition or advanced liver disease) the limit is 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours.
Hypovolemic hyponatremia is treated with isotonic fluid, and overcorrection is common once volume is restored and antidiuretic hormone is suppressed; sodium is checked frequently.

output.summary: Hyponatremia with seizures is treated with 150 mL boluses of 3% saline, up to three, aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour [Spasovski_2014]. The rise should stay within 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further day, and within 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours in patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination, including those with hypokalemia [Spasovski_2014; Verbalis_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 121 with urine osmolality 420 and urine sodium 22 (hypovolemic hyponatremia); potassium 3.4; BUN 34 and creatinine 1.6; WBC 18.4 and pyuria with positive nitrite; lactate 7.8 after the convulsion; levetiracetam 18 within range
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, levetiracetam level
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the levetiracetam level tests adherence, and serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium classify the hyponatremia [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.rationale: Convulsions continuing after a benzodiazepine need EEG confirmation of ongoing seizure activity and of its control, since convulsive SE may continue as non-convulsive SE; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.rationale: MRI is indicated when SE is new-onset, unexplained or refractory; here the substrate and the trigger are known and CT shows no new change [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Trimethoprim raises metformin levels and itself lowers sodium and raises creatinine; sulfamethoxazole raises phenytoin levels; carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine worsen hyponatremia; levetiracetam and ceftriaxone have no relevant interaction

action_criteria.rationale: The second-line ASM and the new antibiotic are added to TMP-SMX, metformin and amlodipine with a creatinine of 1.6; the check informs the drug choices [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.label: Literature: treatment of hyponatremia with seizures and correction limits
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not raise sodium by more than 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours: hypokalemia makes her high risk for osmotic demyelination [Verbalis_2013].
Do not fluid-restrict: the hyponatremia is hypovolemic (poor intake, BUN 34, urine sodium 22).
Do not use carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; they cause hyponatremia.
Do not continue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the urinary infection: the isolate is resistant.
required_recommendations: The prehospital lorazepam 2 mg was below the recommended dose and failed: give IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) now and load the second-line ASM without delay [Glauser_2016].
Give 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes for hyponatremia with seizures, repeated up to twice while checking sodium, aiming for a rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour [Spasovski_2014].

Limit the sodium rise to 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because hypokalemia (K 3.4) raises the risk of osmotic demyelination; check sodium every 2 to 4 hours, replace potassium (which also raises sodium) and watch for overcorrection once volume is restored [Verbalis_2013].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), her maintenance drug; avoid fosphenytoin because sulfamethoxazole raises phenytoin levels and loading risks hypotension with amlodipine, and do not use carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, which cause hyponatremia [ESETT_2019].

Stop trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (resistant isolate, and trimethoprim lowers sodium) and start IV ceftriaxone for the urinary sepsis after blood and urine cultures, adjusted to the susceptibilities.
Hold metformin (creatinine 1.6, lactate 7.8) and dose levetiracetam maintenance by creatinine clearance.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

patient.chief_complaint: Daughter found mother having continuous seizure for >20 minutes at home

past_medical_history: Ischemic stroke 3 years ago (right MCA territory, residual left arm weakness)

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Johnson is a 72-year-old retired teacher with post-stroke epilepsy on levetiracetam who is brought by ambulance after her daughter found her having a continuous seizure. The daughter arrived at her mother's home for a routine Sunday visit and found her on the living room floor in active convulsions. She estimated the seizure had been ongoing for at least 20 minutes based on the time she entered the home. She is not sure if her mother took her medications yesterday. The daughter reports her mother has been unwell for 3-4 days with a urinary tract infection treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole started 4 days ago, which she got from her primary care doctor via telephone. She has had poor oral intake and was possibly dehydrated. The patient has a known right MCA stroke territory residual with left arm weakness. On EMS arrival, continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity was present. Paramedics gave lorazepam 2 mg IV en route without termination. She arrived in active SE, now 25 minutes total. She is also on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and metformin.
